facts.claim: "Thank You" is the 13th and final track on Bombadil's album Metrics of Affection, released July 23, 2013 on Ramseur Records. It runs 4:16.

Discogs credits the writing of the album to Bombadil as a group. Performers are Bryan Rahija, Daniel Michalak, James Phillips and Stuart Robinson. Other credits include Christy Jean Smith on harmony vocals, cellists Elizabeth Marshall and Leah Gibson, and Michael Stipe on trumpet (not specified for this track).
Discogs credits the album's recording to Brad Womack, James Phillips and Jason Richmond. Karl Kling mixed it (Phil Torres did an initial mix) and Dave Harris mastered it.
The band produced the album themselves and recorded it at home. The Salisbury Post singles out "Thank You" as Stuart Robinson's closing song, with the vocal floating over a softly churning piano.

Drummer James Phillips said the album was made by the band together over two months in the summer of 2012 in a big house in Durham, NC. He said it was the first time they used drum machines and described its songs as being about approaching 30, relationships beginning and ending, and finding your place in the world.
Phillips also engineered the album in a home studio. He said the band sees the studio as a place to try anything, and if everyone likes it, it sticks.

The Lyrics of "Thank You" tell the listener to stay gracious toward those who stuck around, and to write down everyone they love and let them know they care. A reviewer called it a sincere, intimate piano song that is funny and sincere at once.
Charlotte's Creative Loafing called the closer a summation of Bombadil's most powerful parts. It said the song is about self-worth and acknowledging those who care for you.
The album came after founding member Daniel Michalak's long-term nerve injury, which limited the use of his hands and put the band's future in question. He recovered and the band toured in 2012.
Bombadil is a Durham, North Carolina band named for J.R.R. Tolkien's Tom Bombadil. Michalak and Robinson take turns singing lead on the album, and guitarist Bryan Rahija later left the band.
A live demo recorded at a campus concert got the band signed to Ramseur Records, which released a self-titled EP in 2006, then the albums A Buzz, A Buzz (2008) and Tarpits and Canyonlands (2009).

research.lineage: Bombadil sits in North Carolina's Durham indie folk-pop scene, with whimsical, literate songwriting that blends folk, pop and piano balladry with some classical and hip-hop touches.

draft:
**Thank You** is a list of advice that keeps interrupting itself. It starts like a commencement speech: forget the ones who let you down, stay gracious toward the ones who stuck around, believe in yourself even if your own mother starts to doubt you. Then it tells you to write down everyone you love and immediately thinks better of it: "You might not want to tell all of them because that could weird some people out." That hedge is the whole song in small. It wants to say the big, open-hearted thing, and it can't stop noticing how awkward the big, open-hearted thing sounds out loud.

The humor never cancels the feeling. It's how the feeling gets through. When the song tells you to apologize to the one you love, it allows that he might not forgive you: "And if he doesn't, well, fuck him, you've done all you can." It's funny because it's honest about the limit of trying. The prayer verse works the same way. Pray every night, it says, though not necessarily to God, because it helps sort your thoughts, "and you never know, they might be right." Then comes the line that drops the joking: "So, if I'm remembered, I'm remembered realistically." Asking whether you'd say nice things at a funeral or tell the truth is a small, real fear: being loved for a version of yourself that isn't quite you. The song would rather be seen accurately than flattered.

Against all that hedging, the chorus is plain gratitude: thank you for staying by my side, what a wonderful feeling to know everything is fine. By the last pass the "wonderful feeling" lines double up, as if the singer finally stopped qualifying and just let it repeat.

The sound is gentle. Fingerpicked acoustic guitar and a clean electric guitar roll through arpeggios over plucked bass and drums kept light with a brushed feel. The tempo sways. The lead voice is clear, with a light vibrato, and a second voice comes in for close two-part harmony. The room is warm, with a natural reverb. The Salisbury Post heard the vocal floating over softly churning piano. It's polished, but not fussy.

Bombadil made *Metrics of Affection* themselves over two months in the summer of 2012, in a big house in Durham, North Carolina. James Phillips engineered it at home, and he described the songs as being about approaching 30, relationships beginning and ending, and finding your place. The record followed Daniel Michalak's long nerve injury, which limited the use of his hands and left the band's future in doubt. The Post singled this closer out as Stuart Robinson's song. Charlotte's Creative Loafing called it a summation of the band's most powerful parts. That fits the Durham folk-pop strain Bombadil works in: literate, whimsical, willing to be goofy right up to the point where it means it.

By the end, the song has talked itself out of its own embarrassment, and it leaves you wanting to thank somebody out loud, weird or not.
